pr_comments:
> I think we are adding more complexity that is a sibling feature to [fastify.io/docs/latest/Reference/Server/#schemacontroller](https://www.fastify.io/docs/latest/Reference/Server/#schemacontroller) (i.e. the goal is already possible by a feature already included).

Well, is kinda possible by providing the SchemaController, as you can store the reference somewhere and just decorate the `Request` with the function you want, but that requires overwriting the `SchemaController` by providing one by yourself, then in case the developer is not interested in using a custom validation library but the default one provided by Fastify, is not so easy to achieve.

The only reason I didn't go in that way was because of the encapsulation, as one of the easiest ways to do so is just exposing the SchemaController and allowing the implementation to do whatever it wants with it. But stills, as Fastify allows to not only overwrite the controller within an encapsulated context but also at a route level, the number of combinations and cases increases.
So my idea was just to keep everything as it is and intercept the SchemaController to provide a smaller function that validates/serializes on runtime, respecting whatever customization has been by the implementation and any level

> Can you please add a unit test?

@mcollina I’ll follow @Eomm suggestion and create a standalone file just for testing the new methods. I’ll use his suggestion for create many tests as I can think off at different context levels
Sorry for being like a ghost lately. Changed jobs, and laptop so I'm needing some time to setup everything once again. I hope to bring more activity to it by the end of the week 🙂

Sure! I think we can go and apply the suggestions from @mcollina and open a separate PR where we can discuss more in big detail an improvement in the shape of the caching, as because of what you already stated, it's easy for the user to implement it in such way that they will never benefit for the cache. 

I think as a first iteration just documenting what's the best approach can help to see how everything goes on a first run meanwhile improving that feature specific 🙂 

Thankfully I'm free from Tomorrow on so I'll start adding the missed documentation, applying suggestions, and also adding the TS types. Sorry for the delay, has been a rough week.
Please feel free to have a look, I think is good to go in this state. Just the documentation is missed, I'll add it Tomorrow 🙂
Coverage is low, let me take a look 👍

issue_context.title: Make available the data validation method with the specified schema and the data serialization method with the specified schema
comments: Would you like to send a Pull Request to address this issue? Remember to add unit tests.

> @zekth I think it is what you need in `fastify-websocket`. I agree to expose the compiler, it is useful for anyone who want to compile their custom validating function.
> 
> One concern only, the compiler should be on `FastifyInstance` instead of `FastifyRequest`.

Indeed this is what we need 👍
unfortunately, I'm not so well versed in the philosophy and internal architecture of fastify that I'm afraid I won't be able to do a good PR :(

I was doing a quick assessment to start working on this and it seems to be doable but will require a few changes here and there, mostly due to the fact that the Serialization and Validator compilers are made with an abstraction on top. This is to bring power to set up granular validators/serializators based on HTTP parts of a request (like `method` and `path`).

And this is even abstracted within the defaults of fastify thanks to [fast-json-stringify-compiler](https://github.com/fastify/fast-json-stringify-compiler) and [ajv-compiler](https://github.com/fastify/ajv-compiler), and they're transparent to which validation compiler are using, making it opaque to fastify being able to return a specific instance of a compiler (either serializer or validator).

One thing that can be done is to make this based on **per-request only**, meaning that we can follow the initial suggestion from @budarin and respect any kind of custom implementation made by the implementation at a route or general level.

**Note**:
- The SchemaController is made based on the same abstraction based on the parts of an HTTP request.

If all agree, I can prepare something soon 🙂

> One thing that can be done is to make this based on per-request only

Not really follow what it means by `pre-request only`. 
I think both the validate and serialize function should be cached once it passed to `.serialize(<schema>, <json>)` or `.validate(<schema>, <json>)`.
If it is `pre-request only` that means the function will be dropped once the request end.

I don't think someone would use difference schema inside same route. But an option to determine if the function is `one-off` seems interesting. It can support dynamic schema from input if someone need.

> We can even use the schema provided as the key for caching the returned function using a WeakMap for it. But providing two inputs will complicate the things, wdyt?

Good.

@budarin 
>May be it is necessary to provide a compiler so that the schema is not compiled every call over and over again?

Can also be a way to go, but that will require quite a number of changes to the way the schemas are handled and stored within Fastify because the way this is abstracted creates the dependency of always providing the different parts of an HTTP request (e.g. Headers, Path, Method).
As for the default implementation of fastify, this is not a problem, but for custom implementations that heavily depend on those parameters to decide how to compile the validation/serialization function, it becomes a problem (e.g. [fastify-split-validator](https://github.com/metcoder95/fastify-split-validator)).

Along with that, [Ajv](https://ajv.js.org/guide/getting-started.html#basic-data-validation) already takes care of caching:
>Ajv compiles schemas to functions and caches them in all cases (using the schema itself as a key in a Map) so that the next time the same schema object is used it won't be compiled again.


So, aggregating all of the discussion here, I'll prepare a PR for this week with a PoC 🙂

I would add a getter here:
https://github.com/fastify/ajv-compiler/blob/bbc98b83ecdc98826c2b621cc9aaa4bada21f3ff/index.js#L36

I think the user must be aware that the instance has all the `addSchema()` references, so if the dev thinks to run code like this:

```
  const input = await (await fetch(`https://example.com/${req.body.id}`))).json()
  const result = req.validate(subSchema, input); 
```

the dev must be aware that:

- the subSchema is not compiled, so it will be slow (compile + run)
- the ajv instance may face `$id`s conflicts

> I would add a getter here: [fastify/ajv-compiler@`bbc98b8`/index.js#L36](https://github.com/fastify/ajv-compiler/blob/bbc98b83ecdc98826c2b621cc9aaa4bada21f3ff/index.js#L36)

That will work for the defaults but not when the route has custom `validatorCompiler`/`serializerCompiler`, as `ajv-compiler` is not aware of such customization, isn't it? Unless I'm missing something, an abstraction on fastify still will be needed to handle such cases.

> I think the user must be aware that the instance has all the `add schema()` references, so if the dev thinks to run code like this:
> 
> ```
>   const input = await (await fetch(`https://example.com/[](https://example.com/)${req.body.id}`))).json()
>   const result = req.validate(subSchema, input); 
> ```
> 
> the dev must be aware that:
> 
> * the subSchema is not compiled, so it will be slow (compile + run)
> * the ajv instance may face `$id`s conflicts

That would be super nice to add the docs for awareness. That being said, I also think that adding the schema to the ajv instance for further references and implementing caching as suggested can somehow lower the overhead but not fix it at all, that is still in the dev's hands.

Please correct me if I'm doing a wrong assumption 🙂

Why is it not acceptable to supply your own schema container? The feature was added specifically to make it easy to work with schemas in whatever way the developer wants while utilizing them within Fastify.

review_comments:
I think we could use the httpPart instead.
For example, user sets the route's body schema.
Then the user wants to use that schema, we could support:

```
req.validate(myObjeck, 'body')
```

So we will use the req's body schema to validate the input obj.

Actually it's already covered as you can see in test [`request-validate.test.js`](https://github.com/fastify/fastify/pull/3970/files#diff-5a65d1f2fa8e4a550dcee897885cb9ddbf3c296dd85bbac9967a2757f2922266R375). 

But is true that it wasn't fully covered as it was depending that schema was not `null`. Change applied as per your next comment.
